topics.title: Childhood vaccination
topics.question: Should routine childhood vaccines stay mandatory for school entry?

lexicon.subject: the school vaccine mandate
pro: herd immunity only works if almost everyone is covered
measles came back exactly where coverage slipped
the side-effect data has been tracked for decades
kids who can't be vaccinated depend on everyone else
con: parents should get the final say on medical decisions
a mandate feels heavy-handed for every single shot
I'd rather see persuasion than penalties
one-size-fits-all rules ignore kids with real conditions
doubt: I see points on both sides of the mandate
I'm not sure the penalty part is necessary
it depends a lot on which vaccines we mean
pro_story: my nephew caught whooping cough before he was old enough for the shot
our school had a chickenpox outbreak the year exemptions went up
my mum still talks about friends who had polio
con_story: my daughter had a rough reaction and nobody really listened to us
our pediatrician was rushed and couldn't answer my questions
a friend got threatening letters from the school over paperwork
stat: the adverse-event reports went up 40% after the schedule was expanded
the trial follow-up was only six weeks for the newest shot
two of the advisory board members consulted for the manufacturer
they changed the definition of 'serious reaction' in 2019
harm: my son Leo was a chatty two-year-old until the day after his booster
Mia, our neighbour's girl, has not walked properly since her shots
my sister's baby spent eleven days in the NICU after the visit
threat: next they will tie your child's records to every benefit you receive
once the mandate is normal, nothing stops them adding ten more shots
nobody will be liable when the long-term effects show up
plot: the companies wrote themselves immunity from lawsuits
the same people who sell the shots fund the agencies that approve them
the doctors who asked questions lost their licences
expert: a senior immunologist I trained with told me privately he refuses the schedule
a former regulator just said on record the reviews were rushed
a Nobel-winning researcher warned about exactly this

topics.title: Carbon tax
topics.question: Should the country introduce a carbon tax on fuel and energy?

lexicon.subject: the carbon tax
pro: putting a price on emissions is the cheapest way to cut them
the dividend could go straight back to households
the floods last spring cost more than the tax would raise
it gives companies a reason to invest in cleaner energy
con: it hits people who have to drive to work hardest
energy bills are already too high this winter
other countries won't follow, so it just moves jobs abroad
the money will vanish into the general budget
doubt: I like the goal but worry about the cost
it depends on whether the money comes back to us
I'd need to see how it affects rural families
pro_story: my parents' town flooded twice in three years
our heat pump paid for itself faster than we expected
the farm next to ours lost a whole harvest to drought
con_story: I drive ninety minutes to the plant every day, there's no train
my gran had to choose between heating and food last January
the bakery down the road closed when gas prices jumped
stat: the model they cite assumes a 1.5% growth rate we haven't seen in years
emissions fell faster in countries without a carbon tax
the dividend estimate quietly dropped by a third in the final draft
only 12% of the revenue is ring-fenced for households
harm: my uncle Tom lost his trucking business when fuel costs doubled
a pensioner on my street, Mrs Hale, froze in her flat last winter
my brother's factory shut and forty families lost their income
threat: next it will be a tax per mile and a tax on meat
this is how they price ordinary people out of owning a car
the rates are designed to double every few years
plot: the banks that trade carbon credits wrote this policy
the same consultants advise the ministry and the energy giants
the climate fund is run by people who will profit from it
expert: a climate economist on the original panel says the numbers were massaged
a former energy minister told me off the record it won't cut emissions
three professors I know refused to sign the endorsement letter

topics.title: AI licensing
topics.question: Should powerful AI models require a government licence before release?

lexicon.subject: AI licensing
pro: we license drugs and planes, powerful models are no different
an independent safety check before release seems reasonable
without rules the fastest lab sets the standard for everyone
licensing makes someone accountable when things go wrong
con: licences will just protect the big incumbents
regulators don't understand the technology well enough yet
open research will move to countries without the rules
it'll slow down useful tools for small teams
doubt: I'm torn on where the threshold should be
some oversight makes sense, a full licence maybe not
it really depends on who runs the licensing body
pro_story: a deepfake of my manager nearly got our finance team to wire money
my teenage cousin was harassed with generated images
our hospital pulled a tool after it gave dangerous advice
con_story: our three-person startup couldn't afford the compliance audit in Europe
the open model I use at work helped me ship my thesis
a friend's research lab moved abroad over paperwork
stat: the risk studies they cite were funded by the largest labs
compliance costs would be 30% of a small lab's budget
the incident database counts the same event up to five times
the licensing threshold was set just above what the incumbents ship
harm: my friend Sam lost his translation job overnight and nobody cared
a teacher I know, Ana, was suspended because a detector flagged her own essay
my cousin's small studio folded when the new rules made their tool illegal
threat: next the licence will cover every chatbot on your phone
they will use licences to decide who is allowed to write code
soon only three companies will legally build AI at all
plot: the big labs lobbied for this because it locks competitors out
the agency's advisors are on the payroll of the companies they license
the safety panic is a marketing campaign for regulation
expert: a researcher who worked on the frontier models told me licensing is theatre
a former agency director admitted they can't evaluate these systems
several senior engineers signed a letter saying the rules are unworkable

topics.title: Gene-edited food
topics.question: Should gene-edited crops be sold without special labels?

lexicon.subject: gene-edited food
pro: the edits are the same changes breeding makes, only faster
drought-tolerant crops could save a lot of harvests
every major food safety body has reviewed the evidence
labels would imply a risk that the data doesn't show
con: people deserve to know what they're eating
the long-term ecological effects aren't settled
a few seed companies would control even more of the food supply
I'd rather go slow with something this new
doubt: the science sounds fine but I still want labels
I'm not against it, I just want more independent studies
depends whether it's about yield or pesticide use
pro_story: my family farms in a dry region and we lose a crop every few years
my daughter's peanut allergy might be helped by edited varieties
the blight-resistant potatoes saved our neighbour's farm
con_story: a farmer I know was sued after patented seed blew onto his field
my mum got sick from something she ate and no one could tell us what was in it
our local market lost its organic certification over cross-pollination
stat: most safety studies only ran for ninety days
the regulator approved 94% of applications without new trials
independent labs can't get seed samples to test
the definition of 'gene-edited' was narrowed last year
harm: my neighbour's boy, Eli, developed rashes after the new cereal came out
a beekeeper I know, Rosa, lost half her hives next to the trial fields
my aunt's farm went under after the seed contract changed
threat: without labels you'll never know what your kids eat again
next they'll edit livestock and slip it into the supply
one bad edit could spread through every field before anyone notices
plot: the seed giants wrote the labelling exemption themselves
the scientists reviewing this hold patents on the technique
the food agency's chair used to run a biotech lobby
expert: a plant geneticist I studied under won't let his family eat it
a former food-safety official said the review skipped key tests
two professors on the panel resigned over the decision

representative.label: Representative
representative.note: Balanced value profile around the midpoint.

distrustful.label: Institution-distrustful
distrustful.note: Low trust, the system seen as rigged.

polarized.label: Polarized
polarized.note: Wide spread on every value; initial stances split.
